title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
lead: Check that a rule gives a definite result and finishes.
why: The properties of algorithms reveal problems before a program is run: ambiguous instructions, unreachable termination and solutions that work for just one sample.
objectives: State preconditions, postconditions and algorithm steps.
Distinguish definiteness, discrete steps, generality and termination.
Trace the program state after each step.
Describe how invariants and decreasing measures support correctness reasoning.
prerequisites: You can identify a problem's inputs and outputs.
Division with remainder helps but C++ syntax is not a prerequisite.

concepts.definition: The intended action of each step is unambiguous.
A property that remains true across specified state transitions.
A property that must hold when the algorithm finishes.
A well-founded quantity that decreases as execution makes progress.

sections.title: Turn an informal task into precise steps
paragraphs: An instruction such as 'repeat until the number is small' leaves 'small' undefined. An algorithm needs an explicit condition, state update and result.
We can state a Euclidean step precisely: while b is not zero, replace (a,b) by (b,a modulo b). With a suitable input domain, a programmer can implement and test the process.

sections.title: Definiteness and discreteness
paragraphs: Discreteness means reasoning about a computation as a sequence of individual steps. Definiteness means the executor can identify the intended operation at each step.
Different programming languages may implement the same algorithm. Precise transitions let us trace intermediate states and compare implementations.

sections.title: Termination, the input domain and generality
paragraphs: A terminating algorithm must finish for every input in its stated domain. A condition such as n >= 0 matters: a loop designed for positive counts may misbehave outside that domain.
Generality means solving a class of related instances, not a single hard-coded example. A sound addition algorithm should work for multiple valid pairs.

sections.title: Correctness requires more than stopping
paragraphs: A program may halt quickly and still produce the wrong result. We must establish both a terminating process and a postcondition satisfied by its output.
In Euclid's algorithm, replacing (a,b) with (b,a mod b) preserves the greatest common divisor; when b becomes zero, a is the answer. This illustrates invariant-based reasoning.

sections.title: Identify an exit condition before coding the loop
paragraphs: A nonnegative quantity that strictly decreases often explains termination. But you must check that each transition actually reduces the quantity under the preconditions.
Changing a loop requires revisiting its invariant and exit condition. Forgetting to update a counter can turn a correct finite loop into an infinite one.

sections.title: Contract and postcondition
paragraphs: For 125 seconds, the result is 2 minutes and 5 seconds: 125 = 60·2 + 5. Zero produces 0 and 0. The general postcondition is seconds = 60·minutes + remainder with 0 ≤ remainder < 60. Integer / gives the quotient and % the remainder. Once nonnegative input has been checked, these operations match ordinary division.

sections.title: Input policy and execution limits
paragraphs: Integer inputs must fit the Code Studio int type. Failed extraction (text instead of a number or end of input) produces invalid; no further calculation is performed.

Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

clarity.goal: Check that a rule gives a definite result and finishes.
prerequisites: You can multiply, divide with a remainder and distinguish starting data from a result. The first topic’s program frame is retained.
model: Express 125 seconds as whole minutes and remaining seconds. A minute has 60 seconds: two groups fit into 125 and 5 seconds remain. An algorithm is a precise sequence of steps for cases like these.

In C++, / between integers gives the integer quotient and % gives the remainder. The divisor is always 60 here, so division by zero cannot occur. Check the result: 2 × 60 + 5 = 125 and 0 ≤ 5 < 60. This is a postcondition, a property after execution.

Our steps execute once, so they finish. A repeating algorithm needs a separate reason to finish: for example, one fewer item remains after each step. A useful property kept by the steps is called an invariant: the processed part has already been counted correctly. Check a concrete calculation before proving a general case.

sections.title: Turn an informal task into precise steps
paragraphs: The instruction “convert seconds to minutes” leaves a question: what should happen to the remainder? For 125 seconds we want two integers: 2 whole minutes and 5 seconds.

Start with 0 minutes and a remainder of 125. While the remainder is at least 60, subtract 60 from it and add one minute. Print the resulting minutes and remainder. Both the step and the stopping rule are now precise.
Predict the result for 59 and 60 seconds before writing code. There are no subtractions for 59 and exactly one for 60. This checks that the condition includes equality.

sections.title: Definiteness and discreteness
paragraphs: Discreteness means reasoning about a computation as a sequence of individual steps. Definiteness means the executor can identify the intended operation at each step.
Different programming languages may implement the same algorithm. Precise transitions let us trace intermediate states and compare implementations.
Reading and checking the range are two separate steps. With oops instead of an age, the program has no number to compare with 120.

sections.title: Termination, the input domain and generality
paragraphs: A terminating algorithm must finish for every input in its stated domain. A condition such as n >= 0 matters: a loop designed for positive counts may misbehave outside that domain.
Generality means solving a class of related instances, not a single hard-coded example. A sound addition algorithm should work for multiple valid pairs.
Try 0, 120 and 121. The same rule must give valid, valid and invalid. Checking the boundary separates <= from <.

sections.title: Correctness requires more than stopping
paragraphs: Imagine the program stops at one minute and a remainder of 65. The total is still 125, but 65 seconds contains another whole minute. Halting alone tells you nothing about whether the answer is correct.

Trace the pairs (minutes, remainder): (0, 125) → (1, 65) → (2, 5). Each added minute compensates for the 60 seconds subtracted. The equality 60 × minutes + remainder = original seconds holds at the start and after each step. A property preserved this way is called an invariant.

We subtract 60 only from a remainder of at least 60, so the remainder stays nonnegative. When the condition becomes false, 0 ≤ remainder < 60. Together with the invariant, this gives the required postcondition. Would the equality alone be enough?

sections.title: Identify an exit condition before coding the loop
paragraphs: A nonnegative quantity that strictly decreases often explains termination. But you must check that each transition actually reduces the quantity under the preconditions.
Changing a loop requires revisiting its invariant and exit condition. Forgetting to update a counter can turn a correct finite loop into an infinite one.

Return to the remaining seconds. Every step decreases the remainder by exactly 60 and keeps it nonnegative. There cannot be infinitely many such subtractions. If you remove the subtraction, the test “remainder ≥ 60” stays true for 125.

sections.title: Contract and postcondition
paragraphs: A timer shows 125 seconds. A report needs whole minutes and the seconds left over. Which two numbers will the reader see?
Write both numbers before running the program. Then check whether they reconstruct the original time.

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and trace the steps
paragraphs: For 125 seconds, the result is 2 minutes and 5 seconds: 125 = 60·2 + 5. Zero produces 0 and 0. The general postcondition is seconds = 60·minutes + remainder with 0 ≤ remainder < 60. Integer / gives the quotient and % the remainder. Once nonnegative input has been checked, these operations match ordinary division.

Division and remainder produce the same result as repeated subtraction. Check reconstruction and the remainder bound. The pair 1 65 reconstructs 125, but violates the bound and is therefore incorrect.
